sources.title: Pandas 101: Loading, Filtering, Cleaning, and Grouping Data

steps.title: Install pandas and prepare dataset
steps.instructions: Run uv init . and uv add pandas (or pip install pandas) in your terminal. Place orders.csv with OrderID, CustomerName, Product, Category, Quantity, Price, OrderDate, Shipped and Country columns in the project folder.

precision_checks.label: pandas importable
precision_checks.command: python3 -c 'import pandas' || uv run python -c 'import pandas'

targets.caption: Install pandas in your project environment

explanations.topic: pip vs uv virtual environment setup

hints: Which package manager command installs pandas into your environment?
Run pip install pandas (or pip3 on Mac/Linux), or initialize a uv project and run uv add pandas.
Make sure orders.csv is saved in the root of your project directory.
common_mistakes: Using pip instead of pip3 on macOS or Linux
Running uv commands without first running uv init .

steps.title: Load CSV in a Python script
steps.instructions: In main.py, import pandas as pd, load orders.csv with pd.read_csv and print the DataFrame. Run the script (e.g. `uv run main.py`) and check the table output.

targets.caption: Load orders.csv into a DataFrame named df

hints: How do you import pandas with its standard alias and read a CSV file?
Use pd.read_csv("orders.csv") and pass df to print().
Write import pandas as pd, df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"), and print(df), then run the script.
common_mistakes: Misspelling orders.csv or placing it in a different directory
Running python instead of uv run when using a uv virtual environment
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df)

steps.title: Create notebook and load DataFrame
steps.instructions: Create and save notebook.ipynb, then load orders.csv in the first cell. Add a second cell with print(df) and run both cells.

targets.caption: Run the second cell to display the loaded DataFrame

explanations.topic: Why use Jupyter Notebooks for pandas

hints: Open the command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P) and create a new Jupyter Notebook.
Save the file as notebook.ipynb, select your Python kernel, and run cell 1 before cell 2.
Put import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") in cell 1, and print(df) in cell 2.
common_mistakes: Executing the print(df) cell before running the cell that loads df
Missing the VS Code Python extension or selecting a kernel without pandas installed
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

print(df)

steps.title: Explore DataFrame rows and stats
steps.instructions: Inspect your DataFrame in notebook cells using head(), tail(), info(), and describe(). Also check the columns and index attributes.

targets.caption: Run summary inspection methods on df

explanations.topic: info() data types and non-null counts

hints: Which pandas methods preview the first or last rows and print numeric summary statistics?
Call df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), and df.describe() as methods, and access df.columns and df.index as attributes.
common_mistakes: Adding parentheses to df.columns() or df.index()
Forgetting parentheses on df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), or df.describe()
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Index DataFrame by columns and iloc
steps.instructions: Select a single column and multiple columns using bracket notation. Use df.iloc[10] to inspect a row and extract its Shipped value.

targets.caption: Index a row and extract the Shipped value

explanations.topic: Series vs DataFrame from column indexing

hints: How do you pass multiple column names into df[...]?
Use double brackets df[["Country", "Product"]] for multiple columns and df.iloc[10] for row 10.
Chain ["Shipped"] after df.iloc[10] to retrieve that single value.
common_mistakes: Using single brackets df["Country", "Product"] instead of double brackets
Using parentheses df.iloc(10) instead of square brackets df.iloc[10]

steps.title: Filter rows with conditions and strings
steps.instructions: Filter rows using & and | compound conditions and numeric comparisons. Practice string matching with .str.endswith() and list membership with .isin() and ~.

targets.caption: Filter rows matching or excluding a list

hints: What operators combine multiple boolean conditions in pandas?
Wrap each condition in parentheses, use & or | instead of and/or, and access string methods via .str.
Use ~ before df["Country"].isin([...]) to negate the membership filter.
common_mistakes: Omitting parentheses around individual conditions when combining with & or |

steps.title: Update values and drop rows
steps.instructions: Update matching rows using df.loc and uppercase the Country column with .str.upper(). Remove a row with df.drop() and verify with df.tail().

targets.caption: Assign updated values to matching rows

explanations.topic: Label-based selection and updating with loc

hints: How do you select both a row condition and a target column when assigning a new value?
Use df.loc[condition, "ColumnName"] = value, and reassign df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper().
Reassign df = df.drop(39) so the dropped row is saved back to df.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning df or passing inplace=True
Using iloc with boolean conditions instead of loc
steps.code:
df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna Ivanova", "Product"] = "Tim"
df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"
df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper()
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

steps.title: Clean missing values and rename columns
steps.instructions: Clean missing entries with df.dropna() and df.fillna(..., inplace=True). Rename OrderID to Order ID with df.rename(columns=...).

targets.caption: Rename columns in place using a dictionary mapping

hints: How do you modify df directly without reassigning the returned DataFrame?
Pass inplace=True to fillna() and rename(), and pass a dictionary to columns= in df.rename().
Run df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True) and display df.
common_mistakes: Forgetting inplace=True or failing to reassign the return value of df.rename()
Passing a list instead of a {old: new} dictionary to columns= in df.rename()
steps.code:
df.dropna()
df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True)
df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Group, sort, and export CSV
steps.instructions: Count countries with value_counts(), sum Price by Country with groupby(), and sort by Price descending. Export with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).

targets.caption: Aggregate total price per country using groupby

hints: Which methods count occurrences, aggregate sums per group, and sort rows in pandas?
Call df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum() and df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False).
Export the table with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).
common_mistakes: Omitting index=False in to_csv(), which writes an extra index column to the CSV
Forgetting ascending=False in sort_values() when sorting from highest to lowest
steps.code:
df["Country"].value_counts()
df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum()
df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False)
df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)
